This is basically nonsense. The 1.5 "goal" was never really something anybody believed was doable. In theory, it was possible, but by the time Paris had happened, it would require such rapid and steep reductions that no nation on earth would do them fast enough. It has nothing to do with millionaires, and everything to do with countries not wanting to rapidly reduce their standard of living. 2 degrees was and still is probably viable, especially if china peaks emissions by 2025, but it too is probably too steep. 

The good news is that the "doomsday scenarios" usually presented as "business as usual" (RCP 8.5 and RCP 7.0) are almost certainly not going to happen as India and China peak and America and Europe slowly decline their emissions over the next century. They literally aren't business as usual scenarios at this point and would require a massive deviation from current policy, that while possible, are highly unlikely for the world's governments to undertake.

I for one hate the emphasis the current ecology movement places on climate change, and how little they focus on land preservation and restoration, as well as micro plastics and overfishing. It is literally, in this case, missing the forest for the trees. Add in their slavish devotion to mass immigration policies that are ecologically completely insane, and I have no love lost for the climate "movement". It's a hijacking of the ecology movement that once dripped in good ol' boy sweat like Ed Abbey's.
paper_abstract: Much evidence suggests that the wealthiest individuals contribute disproportionally to climate change. Here we study the implications of a continued growth in the number of millionaires for emissions, and its impact on the depletion of the remaining carbon budget to limit global warming to 1.5 °C (about 400 Gt CO2). To this end, we present a model that extrapolates observed growth in millionaire numbers (1990–2020) and associated changes in emissions to 2050. Our findings suggest that the share of US$2020-millionaires in the world population will grow from 0.7% today to 3.3% in 2050, and cause accumulated emissions of 286 Gt CO2. This is equivalent to 72% of the remaining carbon budget, and significantly reduces the chance of stabilizing climate change at 1.5 °C. Continued growth in emissions at the top makes a low-carbon transition less likely, as the acceleration of energy consumption by the wealthiest is likely beyond the system's capacity to decarbonize. To this end, we question whether policy designs such as progressive taxes targeting the high emitters will be sufficient
